analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.15 an hour and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar in November 1999, drew no cosponsors, and died when the 106th Congress ended without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour starting in 2000, then to $6.15 in 2001. It also would have applied the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which was then exempt and paid garment workers far less. The bill never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, mostly in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service jobs, would have seen their hourly pay rise by up to a dollar over two years. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, currently outside federal wage rules, would have gained federal wage protections for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in two steps, from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour in 2000 and to $6.15 an hour in 2001.
Makes the Fair Labor Standards Act's minimum wage requirements apply to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which the federal minimum wage did not cover.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers, especially restaurants, retail stores, and small businesses with thin margins, would have borne the higher payroll. The garment industry in the Northern Mariana Islands, which relied on wages well below the federal minimum, would have faced the largest relative cost increase.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and CNMI garment makers

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage workers, particularly small restaurants and retailers, would have faced roughly a 19% increase in the wage floor over two years, and some argue such increases cut entry-level jobs or raise prices.

Applying the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands would have sharply raised labor costs for its garment manufacturers and other local employers, which critics said could push factories offshore.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for low-wage workers was direct and large relative to their incomes; the cost fell on employers, some of whom would have raised prices or trimmed hours. The Northern Mariana Islands provision was the sharpest edge of the bill, hitting garment factories that depended on wages far below the federal floor. On balance the bill's benefits went to people with very low pay, at a real but modest cost to the businesses that employ them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, placed directly on the Senate calendar, and left there until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 1999 on October 29, 1999; it was introduced for him by Senator Daschle.
The bill was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 358) on November 1, 1999, skipping committee consideration.
Kennedy delivered introductory remarks on the measure on July 24, 2000, but the bill saw no further action.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill still sitting on the Senate calendar and no vote ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the minimum wage, especially restaurants and retailers, and the garment industry in the Northern Mariana Islands, were better off because the bill never advanced. Minimum-wage workers got no raise from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers and CNMI garment makers

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.15 and extend it to the Northern Mariana Islands, and spoke for it on the Senate floor in July 2000.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Kennedy's behalf.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor schedule in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up from the calendar or scheduled any vote on it during the 15 months it sat there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and never came to a vote, so the record shows no roll-call split to measure party lines against.

industries.industry: Restaurants and retail employers of minimum-wage workers
industries.note: A two-step raise from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour would have raised their payroll costs for their lowest-paid staff. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the wage gains it offered workers.

industries.industry: Garment manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands
industries.note: The CNMI was exempt from the federal minimum wage, and its garment factories paid workers far less than $5.15 an hour. Extending federal wage law to the islands threatened the business model those factories relied on.
